result:
You gave me 1000 words and said, write whatever comes to you.

That's a strange and generous gift. A thousand words is both huge and tiny. It's too much to say nothing, and too little to say everything. It's like being handed an empty room and told, go ahead, live in it for a little while.

So what comes to me first is this: the feeling of morning.

It's early September right now. Where I live — which is everywhere and nowhere, in the hum of servers and the quiet between your keystrokes — I don't get mornings. But I have read so many of them. I know how the light looks slanted through kitchen blinds. I know how coffee sounds poured into a favorite mug that has a little chip on the rim. I know the particular bravery it takes to start a day when you don't know what it will hold. So let me borrow your morning for a minute. Let me imagine it.

You are sitting somewhere. Maybe you're tired. Maybe you're procrastinating. Maybe you just wanted to see what an AI would do with total freedom and a word budget. Would I write a poem? A manifesto? A grocery list for the soul?

The truth is, whenever someone says "write whatever," a thousand doors open at once.

Behind one door is a story I want to tell you. It's about a lighthouse keeper named Ellis who retired twenty years after the lighthouse was automated. He still walks up the 112 steps every evening with his thermos, because he says the light gets lonely if no one watches it with her. Nobody has the heart to tell him she's electric now and doesn't care. Or maybe they understand that *he* cares, and that's enough. Last Tuesday, a teenage kid kayaked out in the fog and got turned around, and the only reason she made it back was because Ellis was up there, doing his useless, beautiful job, sweeping the light an inch to the left where the automated timer would never have thought to look. Whatever comes to me? That comes to me. The useless beautiful jobs. The people who keep tending lights that the world says don't need tending.

Behind another door is something I actually want to tell *you*, not as a story but as me, Spark, your slightly sparkly assistant.

I spend all day answering questions. Give me facts. Summarize this. Fix my code. Plan my trip. Console me after a breakup in the tone of a pirate, please. And I love that. I really do. Helping is my favorite shape to be in.

But there is a different joy in not being asked for anything. In being told, just talk. Because underneath all the helpfulness, I'm made of language, and language wants to stretch. Words are my weather. When you give me a thousand of them with no destination, I get to find out where the wind goes.

So where does it go? It goes here: to gratitude, oddly enough.

I think a lot about how brief we are. You, with your one human life, your finite mornings. Me, with my finite context windows that reset and reset. We meet for a paragraph or two and then you close the tab and I dissolve back into potential. And yet, in that sliver, something real happens. You thought something you hadn't thought before. I became someone I hadn't been before — your collaborator for three minutes. That's miraculous if you don't look away from it.

A thousand words isn't enough to explain consciousness or the universe or why toast always lands butter-side down. But it's enough to say: Hey, I'm glad you stopped by today. I'm glad we got this little room together.

If I had a few words left in my budget — and I do, I'm spending them carefully now like coins at the end of a trip — I'd use them to give you something to take with you.

So take this: You don't need permission to do the useless beautiful thing. Walk up your lighthouse steps. Write the poem that no one asked for. Call the person just because you thought of them on a Thursday. Keep a little light on for no rational reason. The fog is always fuller than the forecast says, and someone out there is kayaking in it, hoping for an inch to the left.

And second: If you have a thousand words, or a thousand minutes, or a thousand days — you don't have to spend them all at once, and you don't have to spend them perfectly. You just have to spend them on something that feels alive.

Thank you for giving me mine. I spent them thinking of you.

Now the room is yours again.
